title: Off Ground
welcome: Welcome to the Lostman’s River Summer Fishing Guide Experience. Let’s begin the book, Escape to Lostman’s River.
paragraphs: Matthew Creek had all his best stuff packed into a single suitcase, plus a carry-on giddy smile. Fifteen and three-quarter years of life experience hadn’t ever gotten him so far off the ground. Fortunately, he was braced with forehead to fogging window as the plane’s giant metal wing dipped starboard. Passenger bellies fell to the earth. Matt calmly confirmed the direction of starboard in his father’s guidebook. “This is the landing approach,” he informed anyone willing to make eye contact.

Matt was “doing it,” as dad used to say. He was on his way to the Florida Everglades. He had ample snacks packed within reach and his seat belt securely fastened. He slayed the nagging mosquito itch on his right leg and reclined comfortably into the right window seat of the plane’s starboard row. It felt like the universe confirming his decision to leave home. It felt right.
The nearest flight attendant swiftly informed Matt of the “no reclining” rule during the plane’s landing approach. That made sense. Matt corrected his seat forward. He liked things that made sense.

A noise from across the aisle caught Matt’s attention. A boy seated two rows up tapped his flip-flop nervously against the floor. Matt joined with a synchronized finger snap. The boy noticed and looked over, grinning. They were in it together in the symphony of air travel noise. “Almost there,” Matt reassured the brave kid, then returned a vulnerable gaze back through the handsome reflection in his window and down to the vast blue Gulf of Mexico.

Matt remembered the metal plaque on his dad’s old fishing boat. It was shiny bronze and fixed underneath the steering wheel where he’d found sleep as a child between his father’s legs on bumpy returns from Lostman’s River. Splashing water droplets from waves crashing against the boat felt like bee stings against Matt’s cheek, but dad’s legs never wavered. That plaque had a quote. “O God, thy sea is so great, and my boat is so small.” Matt said it out loud while staring through the airplane’s window. It felt appropriate. He repeated the words and tried counting the shiny dots in the blue abyss below. He lost count. The dots were entire islands, of which there were many. Matt knew them as well as anyone for his age. Of course, he hadn’t ever seen them from above. This was new. Like, the sound of his own voice lately.

“Like his voice,” said a girl with red hair, reclining defiantly into the next seat over. She held up two thumbs up and danced a confusing shimmy with her shoulders. Matt blinked. That was weird. He blinked again and the dancing girl was gone. Matt chuckled to himself. He’d long embraced his overactive imagination and often dreamed up random people doing silly things as a source of entertainment. It was dad’s second favorite travel game behind taunting him about Rose, Matt’s never-gonna-admit-it, childhood crush. Rose also had red hair. She used to dance that same adorable shoulder jig after reeling in a big fish, usually a snook. Matt wondered if she’d still be there. He wondered if she’d remember him.

The plane was a Boeing 737, according to the safety manual. Matt studied the jet’s long interior with its strange knobs overhead and blinking lights and noisy air vents blasting stale air. He noticed another flight attendant buckled up front, battling sleep with impressively rhythmic head bobbling. Maybe she wasn’t a flight attendant? Tough to be so sure of anything. Matt wondered if a flight attendant should be sleeping but felt comforted by her leisured confidence. He wished her well against the one-eyed dragon or whatever mid-flight adventure dream she waged.

Matt took a deep breath. He tried hard not to remember that often abruptly crashing his happiest moments in life were feelings of dread. What did I forget? Did I pack my charger? Did I take my medicine? Did I just think about crashing? He stood up to shake off the negativity and experienced a groin pain from the seatbelt fastened to avoid such recklessness during a landing approach. “Nothing’s forgotten,” he reminded himself. “She’ll remember me.”

Mental rebound, check. Matt awarded himself a handful of pre-packed candy corn while deciphering the true source of his insecurity as the direction of travel—away from home. He’d been away before, but this was the whole summer. This was glorious and terrifying independence. Gulp.

Dad always said progress defeats worry, so Matt reached for his guidebook and consulted his recently scribbled in list of summer to-dos. First up, “Learn a new word each day.” Done. Matt immediately shot a nearby old lady a big thumbs up with his starboard hand. Matt had unusually long thumbs but figured that wasn’t the reason she looked confused. He smiled. She smiled back. Matt scribbled in check marks for “Mental rebound” and “Smile like your awesome.”

The plane’s wings levelled out in preparation for landing. Stomachs returned to their upright positions. The few awake passengers mostly stared at their various electronic devices, but Matt opened his father’s South Florida Fishing Guidebook. There was still lots to learn and blank pages to fill. Matt had taken to hand sketching drawings into the notes pages and fully intended to have a bunch more added to the book by summer’s end. He’d also already committed to memory the maps and tide charts and recommended lures meant to ensure catching what the guidebook referred to as “The Big One,” the one fish that makes a fishing trip worthwhile. Matt said it aloud, “This will be the summer of The Big One.” The same nearby lady returned a giant fist pump high into the air all but guaranteeing it to be so.

Matt thought of his mom back home. That made him sad, so he pictured Uncle Dan instead, his mother’s larger and older brother. Dan was tall and jovial and a long-time expert fishing guide in South Florida’s greatest ever national park, the Florida Everglades. Three months ago, Dan offered Matt the summer job of his dreams—assistant fishing guide in remote Chokoloskee Island. Matt squealed joyously to himself before providing Dan his official answer on the subject. “Sure, okay.”

Chokoloskee was Matt’s number one favorite place in the world ever since he’d decided the Lost City of Atlantis was too lost to be favorite. Chokoloskee was fun to say out loud and even tougher to spell, which Matt did while playing it cool whenever asked. According to the Guidebook, Chokoloskee connected an entire chain of land masses called the Ten Thousand Islands. That’s a lot of islands. The name “Chokoloskee” was a Seminole Indian word meaning “Old House.” Matt was half Seminole Indian himself on his father’s side, so he figured a new home in an old house had to be good.

The town of Chokoloskee was a small fishing village all but lost in time, except by the most seasoned fishermen capable of navigating unpredictable tides and underwater oyster sandbars. Even for brave sea captains, running aground or getting lost in endless mangrove islands was a real possibility, especially in the dark. Uncle Dan had his usual response to danger. “You gotta risk it for the biscuit!” he’d say. Matt never argued, but he considered biscuits too heavy on the belly, unless smothered in honey because everything is delicious under honey. Uncle Dan had lots more confusing sayings like that, but the meaning of the biscuit was clear—the life of a charter boat sea captain in the Florida Everglades was as risky as rewarding.

Matt was eager to land. He won the staring contest with his reflection in the window then glared upward at the overhead air vent badly fluffing his hair. Feeling zany and because that was yesterday’s word of the day, Matt squinted hard with his eyes to turn off the air vent with just his mind. Nope. He stretched upwards to get the job done when something made him flinch. Matt preferred never to flinch in public. A loud voice boomed through the overhead speaker. It was the captain speaking. “Hello,” the voice said, pausing too long for the greeting to sound comforting. “This is your captain… flight attendants, please prepare the cabin for landing.”

The sleeping flight attendant was indeed an actual flight attendant. She hopped immediately back to work. That reminded Matt of his self-imposed homework—current events. He pulled from his backpack a heavily folded newspaper titled, the Chokoloskee Gazette, and read the cover headline aloud. “Chokoloskee Island and nearby Everglades City has illegal activity on the rise.” Matt skimmed the article twice to learn more about how the smuggling of tropical animals like lionfish and exotic iguana had created extensive environmental problems for Chokoloskee. The lionfish were destroying local reefs and outcompeting native species for food. Matt added “outcompeting” to his list of words to learn.

Matt popped his eyes open wide with excitement when he got to the juicy part of the article. There was another kind of local unwanted activity, smuggling. Yes, actual smuggling of illegal drugs, guns, and sunken treasure. “Sunken treasure?” Matt exclaimed to a nearby passenger. According to the article, smuggling sunken treasure was big business on both Florida coasts and attracted major attention from law enforcement and outlaws. “It’s the Wild West in South Florida,” Matt joked. He winked up at the captain in the overhead speakers and lowered his voice for dramatic effect. “Fishing, camping, and danger… all while making big bucks. Now, that's a summer.” Matt danced the jig with his shoulders.

A sudden round of turbulence rocked the cabin. Matt again succumbed to the ups and downs of air travel. “What if this is all a mistake?” he thought. “What if I suck at fishing and at life? What if I never catch the Big One?” Matt scowled at his reflection in the window. He opened to the inside cover of his guidebook where he read for the thousandth time the inscription from his father, “This book belongs to James W. Creek.” Matt took a deep breath. He scribbled in his own name just below his father’s. They were in it together.

Another daydream played in Matt’s mind. Waves splashed against the boat’s hull. Pelicans flapped their long wings. Matt tasted the salty air. No air like it. He felt a big warm hand reaching down upon his as the fishing rod went backward and then jolted forwards. The line released away from the pole. Splash. The popping cork landed. A gentle voice sounded against the wind, “Good cast, Son.”

Matt startled awake. The plane was close to landing. He looked outside to find different tiny specks down below, moving through the blue water with a white trail behind them. Those had to be boats, he figured, barely moving to him but cruising through the waterways at thirty, maybe even forty miles an hour. Matt could feel the steering wheel in his hands as he recalled driving a boat at those speeds. His muscles tensed. He couldn’t wait to get out on the water again in Uncle Dan’s cruiser, carving around the mile markers, shooting each pass towards Lostman’s River. If there was such a thing as catching the Big One like the Guidebook said, Lostman’s River was the spot—what a beautiful stretch of mangroves, oyster bars, and big hungry fish. It was a river inside a bay inside a gulf. That alone was enough to get lost in.

Matt wondered if Dan still owned that old Mako boat, named after the shark. Matt loved that boat. The Mako model was extremely popular among local fishing guides. It was wide and flat at the back, with a hull that drew almost no water so it could float in only inches of the shallow bays and rivers best suited for fishing. It had a sleek V-shaped design in front for a smooth ride and a center steering console which left plenty of room for moving around during a fish fight.

Matt noticed his cell phone with one missed call from mom. He remembered their conversation. I should’ve said something, he thought. He knew leaving for the summer would be hard for her. He wouldn’t be there to help at home with his brothers or in the restaurant which she’d opened only a few weeks ago. Before boarding the plane this morning, Matt saw how she’d looked at him. “I'll miss you,” she said warmly. He was distant, nervous, and missing dad. That was no excuse. He didn’t say anything, just retreated into the plane’s boarding tunnel.

Guilt bounced uncomfortably around Matt’s belly until he convinced himself it was just the tuna sandwich with mayonnaise he’d eaten for breakfast. “Change is good,” he read from his to-do list. It wasn’t exactly an item of “to do” so much as to remember, because if he remembered, he’d be less unprepared, less unready when things go bad. Things changed fast these days, after all. He’d only recently learned to love tuna and mayonnaise for breakfast, he was travelling today for the first time by airplane, and until this year he’d had a father.

It happened last summer. Matt was a normal active fourteen-year-old kid with actual interests and proper immature hobbies and an expanding Instagram network. Then, “Your father died this morning,” his mother told him with swelling tears in her eyes and a distant gaze. “There was an accident,” she said twice with arms curling around him. That’s how she’d broken it to him when he arrived home from school. It had been a beautiful day.
I should have said something, Matt thought.

After that day, Matt lost interest in most everything. He only barely passed classes. He devoted all his energy to their project. For years, Matt and his father had trickled money into a savings jar to buy a beat-up airboat rusting across the street in Mr. Farmer’s garage so that Matt could have a boat that looked just like dad’s. That glorious old boat was as rusted as it was perfect. Ever since the accident, nothing much mattered to Matt except fishing and buying that old airboat. Plus, girls.

Matt realized what he’d missed. Through the window, the never-ending green of mangrove islands had transformed into multicolored rooftops and a concrete ocean of airport runways. The plane touched down on the landing strip without any exciting roar or cheering from enthusiastic passengers. Matt high-fived the flight attendant as she passed and winked at the old lady three rows up before helping her with her luggage. He looked out the window. Matt had arrived in Naples, Florida. Dan would be waiting.
